clue.text: Theatre company departs — in a boat?

definitions.text: Theatre company departs — in a boat?

parts.words: Theatre company departs — in a boat?
parts.note: read as 'the cast is off', a troupe of actors leaving; in a boat the phrase means untying the mooring ropes and setting out

explanation.surface: A touring troupe of actors leaves, perhaps by sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'casts' as the cast's (the company's) and 'off' as departed; then the question mark points to the sailing sense of letting go the moorings.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel that lets go its mooring lines and sets out is said to do this; the cast being 'off' also means the actors have left.

clue.text: 100 eggs served up to a party as a menu item

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means written upwards, so the pieces are read in reverse

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
ova are eggs
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A hundred eggs being dished up at a party as one dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' turns C plus OVA into AVOC, then A and DO follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A pear-shaped fruit often served as a starter, so a dish on the bill of fare.

clue.text: Main railway bordering the avenue

explanation.surface: A principal railway route running alongside a tree-lined avenue.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is 'trunks line' the avenue: tree trunks edge it.
explanation.definitionFit: A principal route of a rail network; and the stems of trees standing along the avenue's edges.

clue.text: Payment for minstrel's alfresco performance?

parts.note: alfresco means in the open air, outdoors
a lay is a song or ballad performed by a minstrel

explanation.surface: Asking whether a fee is due for a wandering singer's open-air show.
explanation.walkthrough: A lay is a narrative poem or song, the minstrel's stock in trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Money spent or laid out on something is an expenditure.

clue.text: The, price of two, sparrows Whistler won from Ruskin

explanation.surface: The tiny sum the painter Whistler was awarded in his libel suit against the critic Ruskin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gospel asks 'Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing?' (a farthing was a quarter of an old British penny); in 1878 Whistler won his libel action against Ruskin but received only that coin in compensation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible prices a pair of sparrows at the smallest old coin; and a court awarded the painter just that coin as compensation.

clue.text: A few scouts going the rounds

explanation.surface: Some Boy Scouts are making their rounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scout troop is split into small units of about six; and making rounds to guard an area is the same word as a verb.

clue.text: Provost 'Marshal takes in everyone'- everyone in the street.

indicators.note: takes in shows the military police abbreviation swallowing everyone

parts.note: PM is the abbreviation for a Provost Marshal, head of military police
everyone is all
everyone is all again

explanation.surface: A military police chief rounds up the whole crowd on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: PALL MALL is a famous street in central London, home of gentlemen's clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand thoroughfare in London's West End, between Trafalgar Square and St James's Palace.

clue.text: See us in our distress, so dilapidated

indicators.note: distress signals the letters of 'us in our' are knocked about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A plea to witness our sorry plight, so run-down are we.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fallen into ruin, decayed and broken down.

clue.text: Member yarned in a weird and fabulous way

parts.note: a limb, such as a leg, is a member

indicators.note: weird signals the letters of yarned are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Someone spun a tall story in a strange and wonderful manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabulous in its old sense: belonging to fable or myth, the stuff of old tales.

clue.text: Sturdy finish of hamper nothing broken

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its last letter, here taken from hamper

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
bust is informal for broken

explanation.surface: A strong picnic basket ends up with nothing damaged.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe something strong and hard to damage.

clue.text: Telling the story back in the ring

indicators.note: in places the turned story inside the ring

parts.note: taken as the word ring itself

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word for the story from right to left

parts.note: a story is a tale

explanation.surface: Someone recounting the tale back in the boxing ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TALE into ELAT, which goes inside RING after its R.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrating a story is recounting it, so both mean giving an account.

clue.text: Violent reaction to punishment on the Bounty?

explanation.surface: Mutineers react violently to being flogged aboard HMS Bounty.
explanation.walkthrough: HMS Bounty was the ship of the famous 1789 mutiny under Captain Bligh, notorious for flogging; a lash on the back was the punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong hostile response is a recoil against something; and on a naval ship a flogging struck the sailor's back with the whip.

clue.text: A brownish-crimson banger

explanation.surface: A dark-red firework goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a banger is a loud firework (or a sausage); this sense is a signal rocket fired with a loud bang.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark brownish-red colour shares its name with a loud warning rocket or firework.

clue.text: Tell his weapon? That's a knife

parts.note: William Tell, the Swiss archer, shot with a crossbow
i.e. (id est) means 'that is'

explanation.surface: Asking what William Tell's weapon was, and being told it was a knife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell' looks like the verb 'say'; it is William Tell, the legendary archer.
explanation.definitionFit: A long sheath blade named after the frontiersman Jim Bowie.

clue.text: Senseless, this chess!

explanation.surface: An exclamation that this chess game makes no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: In one form of chess a player plays without seeing the board, keeping the position in their head.
explanation.definitionFit: With eyes covered one lacks the sense of sight; and the chess variant played from memory without viewing the board.

clue.text: Northern gale damage in the East, causing no pain

indicators.note: in puts the northern storm letters inside the East

parts.note: the East is Asia

indicators.note: damage tells us gale is knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A storm from the north wreaks havoc in the East, yet nobody is hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue lost its opening words; the page prints them. 'damage' rearranges GALE as ALGE, and 'in' puts N plus ALGE inside ASIA after its first A.
explanation.definitionFit: Medically, the term means an absence of sensation of suffering, as produced by painkillers.

clue.text: Wood work on stage

parts.note: Wood is the Victorian novelist Mrs Henry Wood, and her best-known novel became a hugely popular stage melodrama

explanation.surface: Carpentry being done in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue ran into another; the page prints only these words. 'Wood work' looks like carpentry but means a work by Mrs Henry Wood, whose 1861 novel was endlessly staged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen (Mrs Henry) Wood's sensational novel was adapted for the theatre and became a staple Victorian melodrama.

clue.text: Occasion of receipt of your come-uppance, Sir?

definitions.text: Occasion of receipt of your come-uppance, Sir?

parts.words: Occasion of receipt of your come-uppance, Sir?
parts.note: come-uppance usually means deserved punishment, but here it is coming up in rank, rising from your knees as a newly made Sir

explanation.surface: Sarcastically telling a gentleman that this is when he gets his just deserts.
explanation.walkthrough: At a knighting the recipient kneels, is tapped with a sword, and rises entitled 'Sir'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial tap of a sword on the shoulder that confers a knighthood; more widely, an honour or award.

clue.text: Plead for poor Enid, put out of church office

indicators.note: the jumbled name is put out round the outside of the church service
poor signals that Enid's letters are in a bad, jumbled state

parts.note: terce is the canonical office said at the third hour

explanation.surface: Pleading for a sorry Enid who has been expelled from her church post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges ENID as INDE, which 'put out of' wraps around TERCE: IN-TERCE-DE. Terce is one of the daily services (offices) of the church.
explanation.definitionFit: To intervene on someone else's behalf is to plead for them.

clue.text: Having made attempt to kidnap queen, hides here for treatment

indicators.note: to kidnap means the attempt seizes and holds the queen inside it

parts.note: a try is an attempt
Queen Anne, the British monarch

explanation.surface: A would-be abductor of the queen goes into hiding to be dealt with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hides' looks like a verb (lying low); it is the noun, animal skins, which a tannery treats.
explanation.definitionFit: A works where animal skins are turned into leather.

clue.text: Natty Bumppo says what he does to deer in the Hebrides

parts.note: the hunter speaking of himself says 'I'
a hunter kills deer, he slays them

explanation.surface: Fenimore Cooper's frontier hunter describes his deer-killing on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: Natty Bumppo (Hawkeye) is the hunter hero of Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking novels; in his own words he says 'I slay'.
explanation.definitionFit: An island of the Inner Hebrides off Scotland's west coast, famous for whisky.

clue.text: Red giant 'almost opposed to war-god

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: anti means opposed to
Ares is the Greek god of war

explanation.surface: A star apparently nearly hostile to the god of war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' removes the final I from ANTI, leaving ANT. The star's name means 'rival of Mars', the Roman Ares, since both are red.
explanation.definitionFit: The bright reddish star at the heart of Scorpius is a supergiant.

clue.text: Great displeasure about pupil "playing hooky"?

indicators.note: about tells us the displeasure goes around the pupil

parts.note: anger is great displeasure
L stands for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: Fury over a schoolchild who has been truanting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing hooky' looks like truancy; read literally it is someone playing with a hook, a fisherman.
explanation.definitionFit: A fisherman plays a fish on a line with a hook.

clue.text: Current form of output from this Moscow club

definitions.text: Current form of output from this

explanation.surface: An electricity generator turns out to be a Russian football club.
explanation.definitionFit: A generator turns motion into electric current; and the Moscow sports club bears the same name.

clue.text: In time oil is processed from stone

indicators.note: In places the reworked oil inside the period of time

parts.note: a month is a period of time

indicators.note: processing changes the oil's letters into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Over time, crude oil is refined from rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is processed' rearranges OIL as OLI, which 'In' puts inside MONTH: MON-OLI-TH.
explanation.definitionFit: A single great block of rock, such as a standing pillar.

clue.text: Mountaineering obstacle Damocles knew about?

explanation.surface: A climber's hazard that the courtier Damocles was well aware of.
explanation.walkthrough: Damocles sat beneath a sword hanging by a single hair, so it was something hanging over him.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock face jutting out beyond the vertical blocks climbers; and Damocles had a sword suspended above his head.

clue.text: Poe's love in particular, and not in general

indicators.note: in tells us the word for 'and not' sits inside the general

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general
nor means 'and not'

explanation.surface: A remark about Edgar Allan Poe's love being specific rather than general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'general' looks like the opposite of 'particular'; it is General Lee, around NOR.
explanation.definitionFit: The lost maiden mourned by the narrator in Poe's poem The Raven.

clue.text: I decry misuse of solid carbon dioxide

indicators.note: misuse of signals that the letters of 'I decry' are wrongly arranged

explanation.surface: Someone condemns the abuse of frozen CO2.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen CO2, used for stage fog and cold storage, sublimes without melting into liquid.

clue.text: Stopping vineyard's return with ease

indicators.note: return asks us to turn the vineyard's word round

parts.note: a cru is a French vineyard, and the 's adds an S
taken as the word ease itself

explanation.surface: Halting the vineyard's comeback with little effort.
explanation.walkthrough: A cru is a wine-growing estate; with the possessive S it gives CRUS, which 'return' turns to SURC.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for cessation, a coming to an end.
